paras: The threatened lynching of the Blalock brothers took place at Columbus, Kansas, in March 1888, when crowds threatened to lynch William and John Blalock after their capture for the killing of Constable David Gordon. Officials calmed the crowd and guarded the prisoners, and the brothers were later tried and sentenced to life. Papers across the country treated the case as notable chiefly because the family's daughter, a local school teacher, was named as a leader of a gang of thieves.

Burglaries, arson and robberies had troubled Columbus and southern Kansas for some time, and residents had banded together and hired detectives without result. Constable David Gordon came to suspect the Blalock family and watched their house after the railway depot safe was blown open.

On a Saturday morning Gordon's body was found near the Blalock house, and according to a Kansas City telegram the shots had been fired from the Blalock yard. The sheriff arrested the father, mother and daughters, and Clara Blalock, a twenty-year-old teacher, was reported to have confessed that her brothers did the shooting. A search of the house reportedly turned up stolen goods and a box of letters, one of which officials said hinted at a murder in Texas.

William and John Blalock hid in the garret of a schoolhouse east of town until a young man reported them, and the sheriff's posse surrounded the building. According to the New York Times account, the brothers came down only after Sheriff Babb threatened to burn the schoolhouse and promised to defend them "against the mob." When they were brought to town, a Columbus dispatch said, the "threats of lynch law" were so widespread that Mayor Chester and leading citizens addressed the crowd and counseled law and order. The crowd promised to abstain from violence, an armed guard patrolled the town, and a large force guarded the parents and daughter in their house.

A coroner's jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against William and Jonathan Blalock, and more members of the gang were arrested. Trials began at Columbus in late April, with Jonathan Blalock testifying for the state against Fred Fry, who was convicted. On May 16 John and Bill Blalock were sentenced to life, while Clara Blalock was discharged for turning state's evidence.

Coverage came entirely from white newspapers, led by Kansas weeklies and wire reports reprinted in Virginia, West Virginia and Ohio. The Emporia weekly news ran the Columbus dispatch under "BROUGHT TO BAY" and called the accused "assassins" and "guilty wretches" even as it reported the officials' appeals against mob violence. A March 23 Columbus letter remarked that "the great wonder is, that they have not been lynched" and likened the gang to the Benders.

Most accounts centered on Clara Blalock, whom the New York Times special called the gang's "criminal queen," and gave the lynching threats only a line or two. The Shenandoah herald reprinted that special on April 6 under "A WHOLE FAMILY OF CUTTHROATS," two weeks after it first ran. No article in the coverage states the race of the Blalocks or of the crowd.
Two copies of the coroner's verdict wire gave the dateline as Columbus, Missouri, but the other reports place the case in Columbus, Kansas.

bases: Crowds at Columbus, Kansas, threatened to lynch William and John Blalock after their capture for the killing of Constable David Gordon, and officials restrained them with speeches, a sheriff's promise and an armed guard; no one was lynched (A1, A8, A9).

A crowd threatened 'lynch law' against the brothers accused of murdering a constable, but the papers report that officials held it off and the accused were later tried and sentenced, so no one was killed (A1, A8, A13).

accounts.label: New York Times special from Kansas City
accounts.gist: The brothers surrendered only on the sheriff's promise to defend them against the mob; the rest of the family was held in their house under a large guard amid threats of lynching.

accounts.label: Kansas City telegram
accounts.gist: Narrates the killing, arrests and Clara Blalock's confession without mentioning a mob.

William (Bill) and John (Jonathan) Blalock threatened; parents and sister Clara held under guard.
Murder of Constable David Gordon; burglary and theft by a gang.
Threats came at and after capture by the sheriff's posse; the accused were in custody and protected.
An excited crowd of Columbus residents, unnamed.

record_check.record: Letters found in the case reportedly hint at a Texas murder...
record_check.dossier: The event was in Kansas; the Texas murder was only a hint in seized letters, not the setting.

info: Constable David Gordon was killed on a Friday night (March 16, 1888); the brothers were captured on Monday, March 19, when the threats of 'lynch law' were made; lynching threats were still reported as of the March 24 New York Times special.
Columbus, Kansas; the brothers were captured at a schoolhouse six miles east of town (or four miles, by the boy's residence in A1).
William (Bill) and John (Jonathan) Blalock, the men threatened; their father William Blalock, mother Ann Blalock and sister Clara Blalock were held in their house under guard.

Accused of shooting Constable David Gordon from the Blalock yard while he watched the house; the family was also accused of membership in a gang of burglars and horse thieves (mail robbery, safe-blowing, arson).
An 'excited crowd' of Columbus residents; no leaders named.
John and Bill Blalock were sentenced to life; Clara Blalock was discharged for turning state's evidence; her father and mother were reported going to the penitentiary.
